damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix – Dumbledore's welcome feast announcement
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Filch as a persistent, rule-obsessed presence whose lengthy list of prohibitions (four-hundred-and-sixty-second reminder) is a running joke that characterises him as a tireless, humourless enforcer with genuine institutional weight at Hogwarts.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Dumbledore begins to relay Filch's customary reminder ('As usual, our caretaker, Mr Filch, has asked me to remind you...') but is immediately cut off by Harry's remark about Umbridge, and the reminder is never completed. Filch's defining recurring joke is truncated to a half-sentence and swallowed by a more plot-relevant beat.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but indicative: the film uses Filch's announcement slot purely as a transitional beat to introduce Umbridge rather than as a moment of characterisation. The cumulative specificity (462 times) that makes Filch feel like a lived-in presence is lost.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix – Filch hanging Educational Decrees (montage beats)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book presents Filch as someone who derives genuine, almost pathetic joy from Umbridge's regime because it promises him powers he has craved for years – whipping students, stringing them up by their ankles. He is vocal about this, gloating to Harry on the marble staircase ('Things are changing around here, Potter') and fantasising aloud about punishments. His alliance with Umbridge is personal and emotionally charged.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film reduces Filch's participation in the Umbridge regime almost entirely to a series of brief visual gags: hammering decrees onto walls, climbing ladders, moving paintings. He is a background comic figure performing physical business. The marble-staircase gloating scene – his most characterised moment in the book – is entirely absent from the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book Filch has a coherent psychological motivation for supporting Umbridge: years of impotent resentment finally finding an outlet. The film strips this to slapstick stage-dressing. The audience never understands why Filch enthusiastically serves the regime, making him a prop rather than a character.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix – Filch discovering Harry in Umbridge's office
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Filch burst into Umbridge's office in a state of feverish, almost ecstatic self-satisfaction: he has obtained the Approval for Whipping parchment, kisses it, talks to himself, and shuffles out faster than Harry has ever seen him move. This scene encapsulates his pathetic longing for authority and his delight at Umbridge's regime in a focused, character-revealing moment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not appear in the film corpus at all. There is no equivalent moment where Filch's desperate hunger for punitive power is dramatised independently of Umbridge's presence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The parchment-kissing scene is one of the few moments in the book where Filch is the sole focus and his inner life – pitiable, darkly comic – is fully visible. Its absence means the film never individuates him beyond a generic antagonist henchman.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix – Fred and George's fireworks, Filch's response
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: During the fireworks chaos the book has Filch actively, desperately trying to help Umbridge: he runs to a cupboard, grabs a broom and starts swatting fireworks, setting the broom's head ablaze. Umbridge shouts at him as though he had cast a Stunning spell (when as a Squib he could no more have done so than swallowed them). This beat is both comedic and quietly poignant – it underlines his Squib status and his slavish devotion to Umbridge.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus shows Filch simply walking into the Great Hall to witness the fireworks. There is no equivalent of him frantically trying to help, no burning broom, no Squib comedy beat with Umbridge shouting at him. He is a passive observer.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book beat simultaneously develops three things: Filch's hapless devotion to Umbridge, a reminder of his Squib status (which makes him both sympathetic and ridiculous), and the comic dynamic of Umbridge treating him as a subordinate who has failed her. The film loses all three in favour of visual spectacle.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix – Filch confronting Harry and Cho in the Owlery
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has a fully developed Owlery confrontation: Filch accuses Harry of ordering Dungbombs, searches him, is stared down by a defiant Harry, and then retreats when Cho witnesses against him – Cho glares back at him fiercely and Filch is forced to back down. This scene establishes Filch as a suspicious, bullying figure who can nevertheless be faced down, and it has downstream plot significance (Hermione deduces Umbridge used Filch as a proxy to intercept Harry's mail).
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene is entirely absent from the film corpus. Neither the Owlery confrontation nor its plot consequence (the mail interception theory) appears.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Owlery scene is one of Filch's most plot-functional appearances: it establishes Umbridge's surveillance network operating through him and gives Hermione a key deduction. Its removal means the film never shows Filch as an active instrument of Umbridge's information-gathering, reducing him from a functional antagonist to background decoration.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix – Filch escorting Harry to Umbridge / marble staircase gloating
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Filch escort Harry to Umbridge in a state of 'extremely good mood', humming, and delivering a sustained gloating monologue about Educational Decree Twenty-nine, fantasising about whipping students and stringing them up, and crowing about Umbridge asking the Minister to expel Peeves. He bows as low as his rheumatism will allow when Umbridge thanks him. This is Filch at his most fully-realised: petty, gleeful, and pathetically obsequious.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent escort scene or gloating monologue appears in the film corpus. Filch is not shown personally gloating to Harry or articulating his investment in Umbridge's regime.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the single richest characterisation scene for Filch in the entire book corpus. Its complete absence means the film never dramatises his core motivation or his almost tragicomic relationship with authority. He is left without an inner life.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix – Filch outside the Room of Requirement (eating sandwich)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book portrays Filch as a genuine, ever-present surveillance threat whom the DA must actively track and evade (Harry consults the Marauder's Map to avoid him; his knowledge of secret passages is described as second only to the Weasley twins). He is a serious obstacle.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus shows Filch outside the Room of Requirement eating a sandwich, snoring, and being oblivious while students file past him. He is played entirely for comic incompetence – he cannot detect the Room at all.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book is careful to establish Filch as a real threat requiring active countermeasures; the film turns him into a buffoon whose incompetence is the joke. This undermines the tension of the DA scenes and strips Filch of the menace that makes him function as an antagonist.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix – Filch after Fred and George's departure (swamp punting)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book describes Filch gnashing his teeth and being assigned the humiliating task of punting students across Fred and George's swamp after he and Umbridge fail to remove it. He also prowls corridors with a horsewhip, desperate to catch miscreants but overwhelmed. He remains the only staff member trying to help Umbridge. This is a sustained portrait of a figure reduced to impotence but still trying.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The post-departure period is not depicted in the film corpus in any way that shows Filch's continued efforts. The swamp, the punting, and the horsewhip prowling are all absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: These beats complete Filch's arc within the Umbridge subplot – he ends up absurd and defeated, yet still stubbornly loyal. Without them the film has no resolution for his character within this storyline.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix – Ginny's report that Filch misses Umbridge
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book closes Filch's arc with Ginny reporting that he is 'really, really miserable' after Umbridge's departure and keeps saying she was 'the best thing that ever happened to Hogwarts'. This is a small but resonant character beat: his investment in her regime was genuine and personal, and her loss is a genuine loss to him.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This exchange does not appear in the film corpus. There is no closing beat for Filch's relationship with Umbridge.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Without this closing line the film never confirms that Filch's alliance with Umbridge was emotionally meaningful to him rather than merely functional, completing the minor tragic-comic arc the book builds for him.

main_damage_causes: The film systematically replaces Filch's interior life – his pathetic hunger for punitive authority and his genuine emotional investment in Umbridge's regime – with visual slapstick and background business, leaving him without a coherent motivation.

The complete absence of the marble-staircase gloating scene and the Owlery confrontation removes the two scenes that most clearly define Filch as a functional antagonist and a psychologically legible character, reducing him to a recurring visual gag.

Filch's role as an active instrument of Umbridge's surveillance apparatus (intercepting mail, monitoring secret passages) is never dramatised, so the audience cannot understand his plot function or the threat he represents to the DA.
